title: World Models Are Not Video Generation: Atlas Makes 3D Control an Input
dek: Language models process tokens; world models process physical space. Atlas's key move is not generating longer video but putting the camera and reference images into 3D coordinates as inputs, turning generation from a slot machine into directing.
why: 23 minutes, medium information density, but Justin draws the line between world models and video generation very clearly. Worth listening for anyone working in 3D, robotics, or VFX.
who: Engineers and founders working on 3D generation, VFX, game engines, and robot simulation, plus investors who want to understand the split between world models and video models.
skip: The opening 0:00-1:05 is show promos and guest introduction, skippable.

points.h: Atlas is a model release, not a product release
points.body: Justin clarifies right at the start: Atlas is not a product, it is World Labs's foundation model; products come later. It does three things — generate worlds that don't exist, reconstruct from real spaces, and simulate inside reconstructed spaces. Generation can start from text or an image, then you directly control the camera flying through that world; reconstruction can use just one photo, or a hundred or more, and the more photos the more accurate the reconstruction; simulation is aimed at VFX and robotics. This order itself shows World Labs does not intend to build a consumer app first, but to establish a horizontal foundation model first and let products grow on top of it.

points.h: Reference images are pinned in 3D space, not fed to the model
points.body: Video models tend to drift and hallucinate direction after about ten seconds. Justin says Atlas's solution is spatial context: the reference images you give are not ordinary images but are grounded in 3D space, and you can specify ‘put this one here, that one there’. When generating video you are not just giving a text prompt but directly controlling the camera, telling it to fly in this direction or that, achieving precise pixel-level control. So even when generating up to a minute, it is not pulling a slot machine — you are generating, directing, and controlling what the model outputs.

Compared with World Labs's first product Marble, Atlas is a completely rebuilt model stack. Marble put Gaussian splat at the center; outputting video, 3D scenes, or mesh all had to go through a Gaussian representation first, then render back to image or video. Atlas breaks that dependency: the architecture is more unified and easier to scale, and the 2D/3D fork happens earlier. When generating 2D or video output, the bottleneck is no longer the Gaussian scene; the model directly produces 2D pixels. Only in applications where you actually need 3D does it lift to 3D.

points.h: Gaussian isn't obsolete, it's just no longer mandatory
points.body: Justin does not think Gaussian has been outgrown; it is just a tool, to be used in the right place. The final product of VFX is a 2D image or video, and may not need explicit 3D at all. But in real-time applications and embedded devices, explicit 3D representations like Gaussian and mesh still have a place: in the future you might stream pixels in real time from a server farm, but we are not there yet, and it would be expensive, so for client-side rendering, mobile, and VR devices, Gaussian or mesh remain useful. Another role is plugging into existing workflows — people in games, VFX, design, and architecture already have pipelines based on 3D representations, and rather than making them switch to fully AI-native all at once, it is better to let AI enter their workflows.

points.h: Simulation fills the last stretch of robot training
points.body: The value of real to sim for robots, Justin says, is first of all evaluation: a robot ultimately has to work in a specific factory, with specific machines, in a specific environment, and you need to make sure it works exactly there. So simulation is useful in the last stretch of training and evaluation — build a simulation as close as possible to the final use case, then either fine-tune a pretrained robot foundation model directly in that simulation, or run evaluations to confirm it works. This gives you a path different from ‘collect lots of demonstrations or human teleoperation’. He also describes a more radical version: take a few photos or casual videos with a phone, reconstruct the space with Atlas, describe the task in natural language, let an agent build the simulation and do RL fine-tuning, and within minutes you have a robot adapted to that space.

points.h: OpenAI dropping world models may be an innovator's dilemma
points.body: The host asks why OpenAI turned the Sora direction — ‘video generation models are world simulators’ — into a consumer product back then, and now doesn't do world models. Justin says he won't comment on OpenAI's internal strategy, but offers an explanation: there may be an innovator's dilemma — you hold something as strong as the LLM and lead in that direction, so investing in the next thing may not be worth it. World Labs's judgment is that there is another class of models here, with a lot of opportunity, and they want to be the ones to seize it.

points.h: Three iPhones produce bullet time, far better than expected
points.body: Asked about hard physics, Justin says he hasn't tried a black hole and guesses it wouldn't be too impressive. But what really surprised him was bullet time: using three iPhones on tripods for synchronized capture, then using Atlas to do a frozen-frame, orbit-around recomposition. He gives the official example — a strawberry dropping into oat milk, freezing time at the instant the milk splashes, flying around it in a circle, and the effect is completely insane. This capability needs only three input viewpoints. This shows Atlas's value is not only in ‘generating new worlds’ but also in turning a small amount of real footage into shots that traditionally required a large camera array.

points.h: 3D is undervalued on the input side
points.body: Justin says 3D has value in two places. The output side has been much discussed — sometimes you just need explicit 3D assets to plug into a workflow or game engine. But the value of 3D on the input side is undervalued: even if the final output is a 2D VFX shot, letting the model provide a 3D control surface helps the director decide what kind of scene the model should output. You don't want to write ‘push in, pull out, move left’ in text; you want to grab the camera directly and make it zoom exactly the way you want — which text simply cannot describe. So Atlas makes camera control a native input type; one of the modalities in multimodality is the camera.

terms.def: A horizontal foundation model based on visual and physical understanding that can generate, simulate, and reconstruct worlds.
An explicit 3D representation that reconstructs a scene using many Gaussian points, convenient for client-side rendering.
Reconstructing a 3D space from real photos or videos, then running robot simulation inside it.
A shot effect that freezes an instant and flies around the scene, traditionally requiring a camera array.
Supervised fine-tuning of a pretrained model on labeled data; Justin says Newtonian physics problems can probably be solved with one SFT.

facts.k: Number of input photos Atlas needs for reconstruction
facts.v: As few as 1, as many as 100+

facts.k: Input viewpoints needed for bullet time

quotes.text: language models are these general horizontal engines for processing streams of discrete tax, discrete tokens. Those have had tons of applications from everything that we know and love today. And our thesis is that there exists another category of model called world models that should be based in visual understanding, should be based in physical understanding that can be used to generate, simulate, reconstruct worlds.
when you give Atlas reference images, they aren't just images. They're actually grounded in 3D space. So you can stage those images in 3D and say, this reference image should be here.
So the idea here is that even as you go to really long generations, it's not a slot machine. You're generating and directing and really controlling what the model outputs.

Marble really put Gaussian splats really at the center of many things that it did. So Marble could output videos, Marble could output 3D scenes, Marble could output meshes, but everything was kind of bottlenecking through a 3D Gaussian splat representation.

I think there is maybe a sense of a bit of innovators dilemma, right? Like you're sitting on LLMs and you've got this as a really powerful thing and you're, you're leading the pack there. It doesn't necessarily make sense to try to invest in that next thing.

I think there's an underappreciated value of 3D on the input side as well. Right. Like even even in a situation like a VFX shot or something like that or the ultimate output is 2D. It's. useful for the model to offer these 3D control surfaces to let the human director figure out what kind of scene the model should output.

you can control precisely where does the camera move because I don't just want to write in text like pan in, pan out, truck left. I want to be able to grab the camera and make it zoom exactly as I like. And there's really no way to describe that explicitly in text.
